entries.title: Iran war: US military strikes Iran's Larak Island
entries.summary: The attack targeting Iranian rocket launchers in the Strait of Hormuz was the first in over a month. Iran's Revolutionary Guards have vowed retaliation. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
Iran

Iran war: US military strikes Iran's Larak Island

Published August 30, 2026last updated August 31, 2026

The attack targeting Iranian rocket launchers in the Strait of Hormuz was the first in over a month. Iran's Revolutionary Guards have vowed retaliation. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • The US conducted its first strikes on Iran in weeks
  • The strikes targeted Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz
  • Iran's Revolutionary Guard has vowed to retaliate against the attack

Read below for top headlines from the Iran war and other developments in the Middle East region on Monday, August 31, 2026.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section US military says latest strikes were 'limited, precise action'

US military says latest strikes were 'limited, precise action'

The US military's Central Command has rejected Iranian claims that its Sunday strikes were an act of aggression.

"US forces took limited, precise action against IRGC minelaying forces posing an imminent threat in the Strait of Hormuz," it said on social media.

"In essence, Iran created the threat and the US military eliminated it to protect civilian mariners, commercial shipping, and the free flow of global commerce."

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps had earlier called the US strikes an "act of aggression" aimed at resolving "domestic problems" and its "diminished credibility."

Skip next section IRGC attacks US air bases in Jordan, Iranian state media reports

IRGC attacks US air bases in Jordan, Iranian state media reports

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it retaliated for earlier American strikes on Larak Island by firing ballistic missiles at American positions in Jordan.

The IRGC said it caused "heavy damage" on what it referred to as the King Hussein base and the Al-Azraq base, both in Jordan.

The Jordanian army said it intercepted eight missiles that entered its airspace.

US sources also said that nearly all of the missiles had been intercepted, according to Fox News' chief international correspondent Trey Yingst.

Skip next section US redirected dozens of ships to enforce Iran blockade

US redirected dozens of ships to enforce Iran blockade

US forces have redirected dozens of ships as part of efforts to enforce a maritime blockade against Iran, the US Central Command said on Sunday night.

The US imposed a naval blockade on Iran in April, after Iran blocked most international shipping in the Strait of Hormuz in late February.

"As of August 30, CENTCOM forces have redirected 83 commercial vessels, disabled 3 and boarded 2 to ensure compliance with the blockade," CENTCOM said on social media.

Skip next section US forces attack Iran for first time in weeks

US forces attack Iran for first time in weeks

US forces reportedly stuck Iranian military sites in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday night — the first US strikes on Iran in over a month.

"Earlier today, US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island," US Navy Captain Tim Hawkins said in a message to the AFP news agency.

"Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz."

Iranian media reported explosions near Larak Island.

The US said last week that it had finished clearing Iranian sea mines from the strait's international shipping routes.

The IRGC said in a statement that the attack on Sunday night "will be answered by the sons of Iran and will result in the punishment of the aggressor."

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to DW's latest blog on the ongoing hostilities in the US-Iran war.

US forces reportedly attacked Iran's Larak Island in the strike on Iranian territory in over a month.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard has vowed respond in a way that "will result in the punishment of the aggressor."

entries.title: Fact check: Germany's Merz misstates record in ARD interview
entries.summary: Migration, debt and electric vehicles: Chancellor Friedrich Merz made several misleading claims in his ARD summer interview. DW Fact check reviewed them live.
entries.content:
Germany

Fact check: Germany's Merz misstates record in ARD interview

August 30, 2026

Migration, debt and electric vehicles: Chancellor Friedrich Merz made several misleading claims in his ARD summer interview. DW Fact check reviewed them live.

As part of an annual tradition, Chancellor Friedrich Merz sat down with public broadcaster ARD on Sunday evening for a wide-ranging summer interview. Amid drooping poll numbers, Merz tried to use the interview to tout his government's work on economic, migration and energy policy.

At the same time, Merz made a number of misleading claims, often overstating his administration's work and misrepresenting climate science.

DW Fact check, in collaboration with colleagues across the ARD fact-checking network, reviewed Merz's interview live. 

Did Merz cut asylum numbers by 60%?

Claim: "One of the main issues in the last federal election campaign was the migration crisis, and together with the federal government, we've been able to reduce the numbers by over 60% in just over a year."

Verdict: Misleading

This is misleading for several reasons — it is both questionable what exactly Merz meant by migration, and also not clear to which period he is referring.

The number of asylum-seekers in Germany has fallen significantly, but not to the extent Merz said. According to the Federal Office for Migration and Refugees (BAMF), a total of 56,547 asylum applications were filed in the first half of 2026, including 39,646 first-time applications. Compared with the same period last year, the number of first-time applications fell by 35.4% — significantly less than the figure cited by Merz. Comparing the number of initial asylum applications for the second half of 2025 and the first half of 2026 with the same period of the previous year, the number of initial asylum applications fell from 169,671 to 91,546 – a decrease of 46 percent.

Comparing individual months reveals significant fluctuations: In July 2026, the number of initial asylum applications, at 4,311, was even around 48 percent lower than in the same month of the previous year. A decline of almost 60 percent was recorded only once, inAugust 2025 compared to August 2024, when looking at individual months since Merz took office .

In addition, the downward trend began even before the Merz government took office in May 2025. After the fall of Syrian ruler Bashar Assad in December 2024, the number of asylum-seekers in Germany declined. At the European level, the number of asylum applications also fell in the first half of 2025.

Official statistics also show a decline in general migration. According to the Federal Statistical Office, around 235,000 more people immigrated to Germany in 2025 than emigrated. This means that net immigration was 45% below the previous year's figure of 430,000 people. But that's mostly due to the number of arrivals falling, while the number of departures remained almost stable.

Germany's debt, in context

Claim: "We are still one of the least indebted countries in Europe. We are still a country that has by far the best credit rating of any European nation. No one doubts the debt sustainability of our country or our economy; we are operating within reasonable limits here."

Verdict: Misleading

There are three important ways to measure how much debt EU countries hold: debt-to-GDP ratio, deficit spending and credit rating.

On the first — debt-to-GDP ratio, or how a country's total debt compares to its annual economic output — Germany receives a failing grade. The eurozone requires countries to keep this ratio below 60%. Germany and 11 other countries are above that limit, versus 15 countries which are in compliance, putting Germany smack in the middle of the eurozone.

On the second — government deficits, or a country's net borrowing — Germany is just scraping by. The eurozone asks its members to keep this figure below 3%. Germany's net borrowing is at 2.7%, joining 16 other countries that are also below the limit. Of the 17 countries that meet that requirement, Germany comes the second closest to hitting the 3% limit.

As for credit rating — a grade from investors on how likely a country is to repay its debts — Germany does indeed earn the highest marks possible. But it shares that grade with several other countries. There are only 11 countries in the world with an AAA rating from S&P: Germany joins Denmark, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden and Switzerland in earning the grade. 

In 2009, Germany amended its constitution by adding a so-called "debt brake," mandating the government to keep deficits to 0.35% of GDP. In 2020, that restriction was suspended to deal with the COVID pandemic and then again in 2022 and 2025 to allow for an increase in defense spending. 

Real CO2 balance of electric cars

Claim: "At the European level, the issue with internal combustion engines has nothing to do with CO2 emissions. We want climate-friendly and climate-neutral cars, but we don't want to dictate the technology — it's not up to politicians to decide that. What matters is how much CO2 such a car emits, and the CO2 balance of electric mobility isn't as rosy as it's often portrayed."

Verdict: Misleading

Battery electric vehicles produce, on average, 73% less CO2 emissions than internal combustion engine vehicles, according to the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT), a US-based nonprofit think tank. 

Battery electric vehicles do generate about 40% higher production emissions, mostly because of the processes involved in manufacturing the battery, though these are usually offset after about one or two years of driving.

Merz was likely referring to a new paper from researchers at the Technical University of Munich, which right-wing media seized on this week. The paper, which took an average of 19 studies, claimed that battery electric vehicles only reduce CO2 emissions by 41%, compared to traditional cars. 

But there's a key issue with the TUM paper: including all those studies means older analyses with outdated electricity mixes are given equal weight. The ICCT analysis, on the other hand, uses a more current estimate.

Either way, there's an overwhelming scientific consensus that electric vehicles are better for the environment than traditional cars.

Edited by: Martin Kuebler

entries.title: Germany news: Merz warns of 'problems' in Saxony-Anhalt under AfD
entries.summary: Chancellor Friedrich Merz said that a victory for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in next week's election in Saxony-Anhalt would seriously damage the eastern German state.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: Merz warns of 'problems' in Saxony-Anhalt under AfD

Published August 29, 2026last updated August 31, 2026

Chancellor Friedrich Merz said that a victory for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in next week's election in Saxony-Anhalt would seriously damage the eastern German state.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Merz predicts 'significant problems' for Saxony-Anhalt under AfD
  • Merkel calls on Germans to 'fight for this democracy'
  • German politicians call for ban on radical AfD state branches

This blog is now closed. Thank you for reading.

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Saturday, August 29, and Sunday, August 30.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Thank you for reading

Thank you for reading

Thank you for reading this weekend's Germany news blog.

We will back with more news in a fresh blog on Monday. Tschüss!

Skip next section Gamescom attendance comes close to record high

Gamescom attendance comes close to record high

The international video games trade fair Gamescom came to a close in the western German city of Cologne on Sunday after being attended by an almost record number of visitors.

Around 368,000 gamers attended the event, 11,000 more than in 2025 and 33,000 more than in 2024. The record attendance of 373,000 set in 2019 wasn't quite reached — but Gamescom is getting closer.

Digital reach was once again substantial, with various online formats recording 624 million views worldwide — roughly the same number as before. On the ground in the sprawling halls of Cologne's trade fair, there were 1,743 physical exhibitions — a significant increase on last year (1,568).

"Gamescom has solidified its position as the biggest event in the gaming world," said Felix Falk, Managing Director of the industry association Game.

"At the same time, the unique atmosphere and enthusiasm on site demonstrated how games forge a strong, creative, and diverse community out of people from all walks of life," he added.

Skip next section Merz: Germany to respond to hybrid threats 'in coming days'

Merz: Germany to respond to hybrid threats 'in coming days'

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said that Germany will respond to Russian hybrid threats in the coming week — in coordination with international allies.

"We're largely in agreement within the government as to how to react and we will make this known in the coming days," he told public broadcaster ARD as part of Sunday's summer interview.

The Chancellor's remarks come following the recent drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport. While an explosive-laden drone failed to detonate on August 5, the incident has put Germany's security and defense infrastructure in the spotlight.

Asked whether Germany was in any position to respond to such threats in an appropriate manner, Merz responded: "Let's wait and see what we mean by an appropriate response."

Either way, he continued, any German response will be coordinated with allies. "Our European Union and NATO partners will not be surprised," he said.

Skip next section Merz predicts 'significant problems' for Saxony-Anhalt under AfD

Merz predicts 'significant problems' for Saxony-Anhalt under AfD

Election victory for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt next week would do serious damage to the eastern German state, according to Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

"Should it come to that, this state would face significant problems," Merz told public broadcaster ARD in his annual summer interview.

"I cannot imagine that international investors would want to be seen attending the first spades in the ground for new factories or businesses in Saxony-Anhalt alongside an AfD state premier," he said.

According to the latest polls ahead of next Sunday's vote, the AfD maintains a commanding lead with 40% — far ahead of Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) with 23%, the Left Party (13%), the Social Democrats (SPD) (9%) and the Greens (6%).

Merz said he would be appearing twice himself in Saxony-Anhalt over the coming week in order to convince undecided voters (which still make up a good 20% of the electorate, according to polls) not to vote for the far-right.

"We will do everything we can to prevent Saxony-Anhalt falling to extremists," he said, adding: "And that applies to the Left Party, too."

Asked how the CDU intended to form a coalition government in Saxony-Anhalt with such low ratings and while refusing to work with either the AfD or the Left Party, Merz said: "We will look at that once we have the results."

The current state premier, Sven Schulze (CDU), however, has expressed a willingness to form a coalition with the SPD, Greens and the Left Party.

Skip next section Hockey: Germany's men retain World Cup title

Hockey: Germany's men retain World Cup title

Germany retained their men's field hockey World Cup title with a hard-fought 1-0 victory over Spain in Sunday's final in Wavre, Belgium. The triumph secured Germany's fourth World Cup crown, moving them level with Pakistan as the tournament's joint-record winners.

Michel Struthoff scored the decisive goal in the 44th minute, beating the Spanish goalkeeper to turn the ball into the net and give Germany the lead. Spain pushed for an equalizer, but Germany's disciplined defense held firm through the closing stages.

Goalkeeper Jean-Paul Danneberg was instrumental in preserving the advantage, making several crucial saves and keeping out all four of Spain's penalty corners. Germany, who are also the reigning European champions, absorbed increasing pressure late in the match to see out the victory.

The title adds to Germany's previous World Cup successes in 2002, 2006 and 2023. Argentina secured third place earlier on Sunday with a 2-1 win over co-hosts the Netherlands in the bronze-medal match.

Skip next section Cologne-Mallorca Eurowings flight forced to land in Paris

Cologne-Mallorca Eurowings flight forced to land in Paris

A Eurowings plane was forced to make a landing in Paris on Saturday evening after steam was detected in the aircraft's galley, the airline said.

The Boeing 737 with 131 passengers on board was flying from the western German city of Cologne to the Spanish island of Mallorca.

The unscheduled landing at Charles de Gaulle Airport was made as a precaution and under "normal" flight priority status, according to Eurowings.

"The safety of the passengers and crew was at no time at risk," a Eurowings spokesman said on Sunday.

Skip next section German politicians call for ban on radical AfD state branches

German politicians call for ban on radical AfD state branches

High-ranking German politicians have advocated for proceedings to ban the most radical regional branches of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.

Defense Minister Boris Pistorius and Baden-Württemberg's state premier, Cem Özdemir, called for bans to be initiated swiftly in a joint guest op-ed in the newspaper Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung.

"We once again strongly urge that proceedings to ban the party be initiated as soon as possible, with a particular focus on the AfD's clearly ethno-nationalist state branches in Thuringia, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt, and Brandenburg," Pistorius and Özdemir said.

Their comments come just days before the September 6 election in Saxony-Anhalt, where an AfD victory could result in a far-right party  leading a German state government for the first time since the end of Nazi rule in 1945.

Pistorius and Özdemir argue that it is important to distinguish between different factions within the AfD.

The two politicians say that the party's more radical, ethnically based wing rejects the constitutional principle. In their view, this wing should be subject to legal scrutiny.

They refer to this faction of the AfD as "völkisch" — a German adjective derived from das Volk, meaning "the people." The völkisch movement was an ethno-nationalist movement and precursor to Nazism. Today, the AfD is often accused of holding völkisch views because its officials repeatedly distinguish between Germans with and without a history of migration.

However, Green Party lawmaker Irene Mihalic warned against a selective ban.

"I see a risk that the idea might eventually take hold that there is an unconstitutional part of the AfD and a constitutional one," she told the Handelsblatt newspaper. "In my view, it is now clear that the entire AfD is at odds with our democratic constitution."

Skip next section British woman stabbed to death at railway station in Bavaria

British woman stabbed to death at railway station in Bavaria

A British woman was stabbed to death overnight at a railway station in the southern German state of Bavaria, police said on Sunday. 

The 31-year-old was taken to hospital but later died from her injuries.

Police reported that a 27-year-old German man was detained at the scene in Rosenheim — the third-largest city in Upper Bavaria after Munich and Ingolstadt.

Authorities are investigating the circumstances and motive behind the attack and have appealed for witnesses to come forward.

Skip next section WATCH: AfD and the battle for young voters

WATCH: AfD and the battle for young voters

For the first time since the end of World War II, a far-right politician could become a state premier in Germany.

In Saxony-Anhalt, the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is well ahead of the other parties, with its lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, especially popular among young voters.

Siegmund presents himself as a fresh and positive figure who wants to "get Germany back on its feet."

We speak to young people in Saxony-Anhalt to find out what they like about Siegmund and the AfD.

To what extent are young people being politicized by the right? Or are they simply disillusioned with the established parties?

Skip next section Three Germans among those missing in Nepal-Tibet flood, China says

Three Germans among those missing in Nepal-Tibet flood, China says

Three Germans are among those missing following Wednesday's flash flood in the Himalayan border region between Nepal and China, Chinese authorities said on Sunday.

A total of 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries were unaccounted for.

Those missing include:

  • 104 people from Nepal

  • 49 from India

  • 33 from Latvia

  • 18 from the United States

  • 15 from Britain and several dozen from other countries

"Chinese authorities have notified the respective embassies and consulates of these countries in China," state media CCTV said, citing officials.

The Nepal Tourism Board, however, said eight Germans are missing. It is unclear if the three German nationals reported as unaccounted for by Chinese authorities are included in the number reported by Nepal.

The Foreign Office in Berlin has said "a high single-digit number of German nationals" are missing in the devastating flood.

On Sunday, the combined death toll rose to 750, with more than 3,000 people still missing, local authorities said.

Several scientists believe a glacier collapse high in the Himalayas on Wednesday may have triggered a tsunami-like wall of water which swept away entire villages in the Himalayan region.

Skip next section Merkel calls on Germans to 'fight for this democracy'

Merkel calls on Germans to 'fight for this democracy'

Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel has called on her compatriots to "stand up" for democracy ahead of next weekend's state election in Saxony-Anhalt.

The far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) is leading polls raising questions about what kind of government will be formed.

Despite this, the majority of Germans are not AfD voters, Merkel said at a political event in Berlin on Saturday night.

"I believe that now, once again — something we haven't had to do for many decades — we must really fight for this democracy, simply stand up for it, be a little brave, stand by our word and say that this is a wonderful way to live," she said.

Merkel said the AfD had, to some extent, managed to "dominate all our discussions from morning to night" about politics in Saxony-Anhalt. This meant that many voters no longer knew the policies of the other parties, she said.

But while the AfD has long polled strongest in the eastern states, Merkel — who herself hails from the former East Germany — said the rise of the AfD was not limited to those areas.

"It has become a pan-German phenomenon," she said.

Skip next section German government expected to hold Moscow responsible for Leipzig drone incident, reports say

German government expected to hold Moscow responsible for Leipzig drone incident, reports say

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government plans to officially hold Moscow responsible for the Leipzig drone incident in early August, several German news outlets owned by media company Axel Springer SE reported on Saturday.

Berlin is expected to announce the planned move in the coming days, including "extensive" sanctions, three officials familiar with the matter told German newspaper Welt am Sonntag and the media outlet Politico.

However, the three sources did not elaborate on what the specific measures could be. It is also unclear to what extent Berlin plans to hold Russia responsible for the Leipzig incident.

On August 4, a drone loaded with explosives was discovered near Ukrainian cargo planes at Leipzig/Halle Airport, which serves as a hub for military aid shipments to Ukraine for its war against Russia. 

Merz told RTL in an interview on Thursday that the federal government would soon identify those responsible for the incident.

Skip next section Sick leave now costs Germany twice as much as in 2010

Sick leave now costs Germany twice as much as in 2010

The total amount of wages German firms paid in sick and maternity leave has more than doubled over the past 15 years, a study from the Cologne-based German Economic Institute (IW) shows.

IW estimated that German companies paid a record-high €85.6 billion ($111 billion) in wages to employees who were out sick last year. This compares to €36.9 billion in 2010.

Of the larger figure, €72.5 billion represented gross wages, while €13.1 billion was earmarked for social security contributions.

IW said several factors have contributed to the rise, including wage hikes and inflation in other employee costs.

The institute said the total number of employed people has also grown since 2010, meaning more workers are eligible for sick leave.

IW, however, said it had noted a "significant" rise in recorded sick leave since Germany moved to electronic medical certificates in 2022.

Separate research by the Berlin-based IGES Institute in January showed that German workers now take an average of 19.5 working days as sick leave per year, a noticeable increase from about 13 days in 2018.

In an effort to stem the rise, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government will from January ban patients from receiving sick notes from doctors by phone. 

In Germany, employers are generally required to pay workers' salaries for up to six weeks before the statutory health insurance fund takes over by paying sickness benefits.

Skip next section Lower Saxony premier seeks deal on VW restructuring

Lower Saxony premier seeks deal on VW restructuring

Volkswagen's second-biggest shareholder has called on all sides to agree on a restructuring plan for the German auto giant in the next few days.

Olaf Lies, state premier of Lower Saxony — which holds 18% of VW's shareholder voting rights — said he was convinced "a viable solution" can be found.

"I strongly urge that we ​use the time remaining until the next meeting to bring the different positions together," Lies told journalists on Friday.

The state leader noted that VW must face its numerous business challenges head-on, namely costly tariffs, falling demand and intense competition from China.

But he said the group's position in Germany's industrial landscape ‌also had to be considered.

"With its sites in Lower Saxony and ‌across ​Germany, its tens of thousands of employees and their families, and its suppliers and service providers, Volkswagen also bears an enormous responsibility for the wider economy and society," Lies said.

VW's management now thinks they may need to cut up to 100,000 jobs and that several German factories may face closure.

The supervisory board of Europe's largest automaker is due to meet on September 4 ‌to discuss a ⁠turnaround ⁠plan.

Skip next section Survey: Trump's return increased US influence over Germany

Survey: Trump's return increased US influence over Germany

Two-thirds of residents think the United States has more influence on Germany since US President Donald Trump returned to the White House.

A poll by the Forsa research institute found that 67% of respondents agreed, while just 11% thought there was less US influence. Around 18% thought it was the same.

The survey for the German-language Internationale Politik (International Politics) magazine found only 2% of 18 to 29-year-olds and 6% of 30 to 44-year-olds think US influence in Germany is lower than before Trump's second term. That's versus 18% of respondents aged 60 and over.

Germany-US ties have soured since Trump's reelection, due to surprise tariffs, talk of seizing Greenland and open sniping over Russia's war in Ukraine and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran war.

entries.title: NASA launches first telescope named after female scientist
entries.summary: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, named after NASA's first Chief of Astronomy, will observe black holes, exoplanets and exploding stars.
entries.content:
August 30, 2026

The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, named after NASA's first Chief of Astronomy, will observe black holes, exoplanets and exploding stars.

NASA has launched a powerful new telescope designed to explore distant planets, exploding stars and black holes while surveying the universe on an unprecedented scale.

The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, named after one of the first women to hold a senior leadership position at NASA, was launched aboard a Falcon Heavy rocket operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX from Cape Canaveral, Florida, on Sunday.

The telescope is expected to reach its destination, approximately 1.6 million kilometers (about one million miles) from Earth, in approximately one month's time.

The mission has a total budget of more than $4 billion (€3.45 billion). The first images are expected back on Earth in early 2027.

What will the Roman telescope do?

Astronomers will use "Roman" to investigate a wide range of cosmic phenomena, including black holes, exoplanets and exploding stars.

"It's going to find thousands of supernovae, tens of thousands of planets, billions of galaxies and tens of billions of stars," said NASA science mission director Nicky Fox. "It's going to be able to do things that we've never been able to do before with its massive field of view."

Roman operates in a similar way to the Hubble Space Telescope, which was launched in 1990 and is now showing signs of age while operating with reduced capabilities.

However, Roman is designed to survey the sky far more quickly and will be capable of completing in just one month observations which would have taken Hubble a century.

Scientists expect Roman to generate more than 500 terabytes of data every year. By way of comparison, Hubble has collected approximately 400 terabytes of data in over three decades in space.

"Roman's vast reach will allow us to find the weird, the rare and the unusual," senior project scientist Julie McEnery said on Saturday. "We'll redefine what it means to find a needle in a haystack."

Who was Nancy Grace Roman?

The James Webb Space Telescope, named after former NASA administrator James Webb, was launched in late 2021 to complement Hubble. Webb observes the universe at different wavelengths, complementing the observations that will be made by Hubble and Roman.

Launching nearly a year ahead of schedule and within budget, Roman is NASA's first space telescope to be named after a woman. Nancy Grace Roman served as NASA's first Chief of Astronomy throughout the 1960s and 1970s, and retired NASA scientist Ed Weiler said the honor was long overdue.

"This is very, very fitting," he said. "I think Nancy would be very proud."

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Germany's Christian Churches take a stand against far right
entries.summary: The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has embarked on a confrontational course toward the churches. Representatives of the Catholic and Protestant churches are responding with a mix of anxiety and resolve.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany's Christian Churches take a stand against far right

August 30, 2026

The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has embarked on a confrontational course toward the churches. Representatives of the Catholic and Protestant churches are responding with a mix of anxiety and resolve.

Flags flutter in the wind outside Magdeburg's Catholic cathedral. "Love thy neighbor, dialogue, human dignity, solidarity. VOTE CONSCIOUSLY!", they proclaim. Just a few minutes' walk away, a sign on the building of the Protestant Cathedral Congregation reads: "DIVERSITY IS DIVINE." Other Protestant churches across the region display banners reading "Heart Instead of Hate."

For many months now, warnings about the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which is particularly strong in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, have been part of everyday church life. During a sermon at a pilgrimage event in September 2025, Magdeburg Bishop Gerhard Feige remarked almost in passing that pilgrims of hope do not cast their votes on a whim, "into the blue." He was interrupted by prolonged applause — blue is the AfD's party color.

The AfD holds a commanding lead in the polls ahead of the state election on September 6. The prospect of a government led by the party alone appears increasingly plausible. At the same time, Germany's domestic intelligence agency has classified the AfD's Saxony-Anhalt branch as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" organization.

Churches speak out against AfD

In Saxony-Anhalt, 10% of the population is Protestant and 3% is Catholic; only a few thousand people belong to the Muslim or Jewish faiths.

More than 85% of the state's 2.1 million residents have no religious affiliation, compared with a national average of 47%. Nevertheless, the churches play an important role as defenders of democracy — and that, apparently, is precisely what troubles the AfD.

With its so-called government program, adopted at a state party conference in April, the party launched a broadside against both the Protestant and Catholic churches. The program calls for an end to all state payments to the two churches and for the abolition of church tax collection by public authorities, a service for which the churches themselves pay.

In cases of so-called church asylum, where refugees seek shelter on church premises for fear of renewed persecution in their countries of origin, the AfD is calling for churches to be held financially accountable on a "permanent" basis.

The Protestant Academy of Saxony-Anhalt should also no longer receive any state funding whatsoever. The reason, according to the AfD, is its "political agitation in line with the established parties: climate dogma, gender ideology, and the rainbow cult." The academy is said to advocate "unchecked mass immigration." Yet in scarcely any German federal state is the proportion of foreign nationals as low as it is in Saxony-Anhalt.

From estrangement to open confrontation

The sharpness of the criticism goes far beyond anything typically heard from other regional branches of the Alternative for Germany or from the party's national leadership. Long gone are the days when representatives of the then-emerging party complained about not being invited to church congresses or Catholic conventions.

In February 2024, the plenary assembly of the German Catholic Bishops' Conference unanimously adopted a declaration entitled "Ethnic Nationalism and Christianity are Incompatible." In it, the bishops identified an ethnonationalist mindset within the AfD and spoke of a "genuine right-wing extremism." The document was prompted by the state elections scheduled to take place later that year in the eastern German states of Thuringia, Saxony, and Brandenburg. Now, in September 2026, elections are due to follow in Saxony-Anhalt, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin.

At present, the confrontation between the AfD and the churches is nowhere more intense than in Saxony-Anhalt.

For Bishop Feige, the AfD's current direction is "without question" an expression of ethnonationalism. "Until now, Saxony-Anhalt's motto has been 'Thinking Modern'. The AfD wants to replace it with 'Thinking German'," he told DW. "The AfD's election posters speak a very clear language: 'Save your country', 'Take your country back', 'Deport from day one!' What else could that be but ethnonationalism?"

The 74-year-old said he "could never have imagined that so many people today could once again be so easily led astray, or that arsonists, pied pipers and respectable-looking agitators could emerge, and that so many would fall for them."

As an example, Feige cited the so-called flag assembly that the AfD wants to reintroduce in the state's schools: the raising of the flag and the singing of the national anthem. "This existed during the Nazi era and was later adopted by the GDR," he said, referring to the former East Germany. "And now it is supposed to return? I find that inconceivable."

Both major Christian churches emphasize they are speaking out not against a particular party, but in defense of a Christian view of humanity. Whether the issue is climate protection and the safeguarding of creation or the treatment of strangers, the churches' interventions are "primarily not political messages, but Christian ones, and should not be interpreted as an endorsement of any particular political party," Friedrich Kramer, bishop of the Protestant Church in central Germany, recently told the online magazine Die Eule.

Religious freedom, according to the AfD

Jews and Jewish life, incidentally, are never mentioned in the government program. By contrast, Islam appears repeatedly. According to the AfD, it will "restore religious freedom to appropriate limits." Islam is described as a "religion alien to our culture." Freedom of religion, the party argues, does not oblige Germans to "fulfill every demand of the Islamic lobby."

Representatives of the state's Jewish association, which includes the synagogue of the Jewish community of Halle targeted in a 2019 right-wing extremist attack, as well as representatives of the largest mosque congregation in the state, declined to comment when asked.

Notably, the AfD's platform speaks of a "Christian mission" that, in its view, the churches supported by church tax, which it labels the "church-tax churches," no longer fulfill. This evokes the support that US President Donald Trump receives from influential evangelical and conservative Christian groups in the United States. In Saxony-Anhalt, however, there is only a limited presence of comparable religious milieus.

Why bishops are sounding the alarm

"A government involving the AfD would have devastating consequences," Kramer said. That is why, he added, cultural institutions and civil society organizations are joining forces to warn against the AfD.

His Catholic counterpart, Feige, likewise cautioned against "downplaying" the prospect of an AfD-led government. During the election campaign, he said, the party is presenting itself "with messianic ideas" and promoting slogans such as "Everything will be fine" or "Anything is possible."

Because the AfD's lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, "comes across as highly polished and enthusiastic," some people ask what could possibly be "right-wing extremist or dangerous" about him. "But behind him stand forces that give cause for concern," said Feige. "If an AfD single-party government comes to power here, it will be a pilot project. Then Saxony-Anhalt will become a gateway to national politics."

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: EU wants drones to spray pesticides — but it could backfire
entries.summary: The EU wants to lift a decades-old ban on spraying pesticides from the air, allowing drones to be used for greater precision. But experts warn the plan could lead to even more pesticides being used in agriculture.
entries.content:
August 30, 2026

The EU wants to lift a decades-old ban on spraying pesticides from the air, allowing drones to be used for greater precision. But experts warn the plan could lead to even more pesticides being used in agriculture.

In theory, the idea doesn't sound bad: Instead of using tractors to spray large quantities of pesticides over fields, drones could precisely spray herbicides, fungicides and insecticides only where they are actually needed.

The plan would be to scan a field, identify affected areas and treat them selectively — significantly reducing pesticide use, according to the European Union's Omnibus X legislative package, which aims to simplify EU food and feed safety rules. After all, the bloc aims to halve the use of chemicals for plant protection by 2030.

Until now, however, the EU had a decades-old ban on spraying pesticides from the air over agricultural land. Exceptions applied only to difficult-to-work terrain, such as steep vineyard slopes. Omnibus X is now set to change that. In May, the European Council gave the legislative package the green light.

Drone use doesn't automatically mean less pesticides

"I think it makes sense in principle to distinguish spray drones from conventional aerial application from a regulatory perspective," said Thomas Daum, an agricultural economist and human ecologist at the School of Global Studies at the University of Gothenburg. Daum studies new technologies and their impact on agriculture. Compared with an airplane or helicopter, he said drones can generally spray more precisely.

However, Daum also cautioned that "the drone itself does not save any pesticide." He sees potential for using drones to respond more selectively to pest infestations — and thus reduce overall pesticide use. Another advantage for farmers could be the ability to respond quickly to an infestation "even when soils are wet or in difficult-to-access terrain."

"At the same time, this flexibility lowers the barriers to treatment and could therefore also lead to spraying being carried out more frequently overall," Daum said. This could result in a technological lock-in — meaning that more efficient application could reinforce dependence on chemical crop protection.

Omnibus X aims to save administrative costs, cash

Chemical pesticides have been cause for concern for many researchers. Omnibus X is intended not only to make it easier to use spray drones, but also to change the way pesticides are approved.

When the European Council approved Omnibus X in May, a group of researchers from 27 European research institutions voiced strong criticism. Among them was Carsten Brühl, a biologist at the Institute for Environmental Sciences at the Rheinland-Pfalz Technical University of Kaiserslautern-Landau. Brühl, who studies the effects of pesticides on the environment, called Omnibus X a "deregulation package" and is deeply alarmed by it.

To date, pesticide active substances have generally been approved at the EU level for a period of 10 years. Once that period expires, manufacturers can apply for renewed approval and must once again submit data on the safety of the active substance. Since this review process was introduced in 2011, it has resulted in 59 active substances not being reapproved, as they were deemed harmful to human health and the environment.

The main aim of the Omnibus X package is to cut administrative costs, reduce bureaucracy and "ensure fair treatment for companies while safeguarding fair competition within the internal market [...]," according to an EU press release.

Researchers warn Omnibus X could harm people, environment

European scientists have been critical of the EU proposal to cut red tape and deregulate the industry, because it could lead to many active substances being approved indefinitely, eliminating regular reassessments. They also say the transition periods after an approval expires would be extended from 18 months to three years.

Brühl called the idea "reckless." It would mean that even active substances suspected of being harmful to human health could remain on the market — like weedkiller glyphosate, for example, which has been linked to cancer in humans.

But the precautionary principle should apply, Brühl argued. This political principle holds that potential harm to people and nature should be prevented proactively, even when there is not yet conclusive scientific evidence.

The scientific evidence on pesticides is already incomplete. The risks posed by an active substance are inferred from the results of laboratory studies, Brühl said. But how that substance actually behaves over the long term under different environmental conditions and in combination with other pesticides is unclear at the time of approval. That is why regular reassessments are so important.

Brühl now fears Omnibus X could undermine scientific interest in studying these active substances. It would be unappealing for researchers "to engage with a system that can no longer be influenced anyway," he said.

Agriculture can work without pesticides

Brühl is certain the new EU legislation will not lead to lower pesticide use — not even with the help of drones and more targeted spraying. This approach, for example, does not work at all with fungicides, he pointed out. Fungicides combat fungal infections and have to be applied preventively because once a plant has become infected, it can no longer be saved.

But Brühl stressed there is another way: doing without pesticides entirely, through what is known as "integrated pest management." And this isn't some hippie eco-fantasy, but rather a concept for the sustainable management of harmful organisms enshrined in German law in 2012.

Shortly after the European Council gave the green light to Omnibus X and its new rules on drones and pesticides in May, the Scientific Advisory Board of Germany's National Action Plan for the Sustainable Use of Plant Protection Products reminded the German government of its own law in a statement. Brühl was the lead author.

Researchers wrote that integrated pest management calls for the use of synthetic chemical pesticides only as a last resort. The goal is to secure yields and quality while also minimizing negative consequences for people and nature and preventing resistance to plant protection products. This can work if certain crop rotations are taken into account and mixed cropping is favored. Pests can be controlled by attracting natural predators through flower strips or hedges, while weeds can be removed mechanically.

The problem: Spraying pesticides is often the less time-consuming and therefore cheaper option. There is also a persistent narrative that pesticides are necessary to ensure food security.

What this narrative leaves out is that monocultures and ecosystems disrupted by pesticides make agriculture more vulnerable to changing environmental conditions. That threatens food security, said Brühl, "because you have a system in place that can't cope with climate change."

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Guinea-Bissau votes to reshape presidency
entries.summary: The West African nation's military government wants to amend the constitution to give more powers to the president. The junta, which seized power last year, says it will hold elections in December.
entries.content:
Guinea-Bissau

Guinea-Bissau votes to reshape presidency

August 30, 2026

The West African nation's military government wants to amend the constitution to give more powers to the president. The junta, which seized power last year, says it will hold elections in December.

Guinea-Bissau voted on Sunday in a referendum on whether to give the president new powers as the country prepares to transition from military to democratic rule.

According to the Associated Press, many polling stations had low turnout after the opposition urged voters to boycott the referendum.

The tiny West African nation of around 2.2 million people has been under army rule since last November following a disputed election.

What will the referendum decide?

Guinea-Bissau's junta has unanimously approved a constitutional amendment to switch the country from what it frames as a parliamentary to a presidential system.

This means abandoning the old system where the prime minister came from the parliamentary majority.

The amendment would allow the president to appoint and dismiss the prime minister and dissolve parliament.

If passed, the new constitution will cut the number of seats in parliament from 102 to 65.

The junta says the change seeks to stabilize institutions before new presidential and parliamentary elections, scheduled for December 6, which are meant to hand power back to civilians.

Opposition groups, however, have urged the public to boycott the vote, saying it will allow the junta leader to cement power and calling it a "source of political instability at all levels."

When are the results due?

Polls close at 1700 GMT on Sunday, with the first provisional results due from Tuesday.

One of the world's poorest countries, Guinea-Bissau has experienced five coups and a series of attempted coups since 1974.

A military government seized power in November following a disputed election in which former President Umaro Sissoco Embalo and opposition candidate Fernando Dias both claimed victory.

After legislative elections in 2023, Embalo himself dissolved the opposition-dominated parliament in response to what he described as an attempted coup.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Ferry carrying over 260 people capsizes off Cyprus
entries.summary: Several people have died after a passenger ⁠boat carrying more than 260 people capsized off ‌northern Cyprus. ‌
entries.content:
Cyprus

Ferry carrying over 260 people capsizes off Cyprus

August 30, 2026

Several people have died after a passenger ⁠boat carrying more than 260 people capsized off ‌northern Cyprus. ‌

A passenger ferry capsized off the coast of northern Cyprus on Sunday, shortly after leaving port, the local government said.

At least eight people have died, Turkish state media reported, citing Unal Ustel, prime minister of the self-proclaimed Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC).

Ustel said some 237 people had been rescued, while 23 people were missing.

He also nnounced that the ship's captain and seven crew members had been arrested.

Cyprus has been divided since 1974, with the northern part under the administration of the TRNC, which is recognized internationally only by Turkey. 

Passenger boat heading from northern Cyprus to Turkey

Turkish media reported that a ferry carrying more than 260 passengers was traveling from the port of Kyrenia, also known as Girne, to the Turkish port of Tasucu in southern Mersin province when it sank.

Erhan Arikli, the TRNC's transport minister, told Turkish and Cypriot media that there were 267 people on board — 259 passengers and eight crew members.

"All necessary preparations are being made for a swift response from rescue and health services," the TRNC's Health Ministry said in a statement.

Search-and-rescue operations ongoing

In a post on X, Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz said: "We are closely following the unfortunate incident that has occurred and providing all possible support to the search-and-rescue efforts."

Turkey's state-run TRT news channel reported that the ferry began taking on water 7.5 kilometers (4 nautical miles) from the coast.

Edited by: Natalie Muller, Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Iceland voters reject EU accession talks
entries.summary: A nationwide referendum failed to win enough support to restart negotiations on European Union membership, despite geopolitical tensions in the North Atlantic.
entries.content:
Iceland

Iceland voters reject EU accession talks

Published August 30, 2026last updated August 30, 2026

A nationwide referendum failed to win enough support to restart negotiations on European Union membership, despite geopolitical tensions in the North Atlantic.

Voters in Iceland have rejected a plan to restart accession talks with the European Union, final referendum results showed on Sunday.

The 'No' camp secured victory with 52.8% of the votes, while the 'Yes' camp garnered 47.2% support, the official count published by public broadcaster RUV showed.

The capital, Reykjavik, was the only area in the island nation of 400,000 people to support the referendum.

Some 270,000 Icelanders were eligible to vote, 82% of whom did so.

Iceland PM: 'Not a setback'

Icelandic Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir, who backed the "yes" campaign, said she did not see her fellow citizens' vote as a defeat but as a fair democratic result.

"I don't see this as a setback. I see this as a victory for democracy," she said. "We had over 80% of the country participate in a matter like this."

She confirmed that her government was "not going forward with the accession talks this term" but that it would continue ⁠to strengthen ⁠its relationship ​with the ​European Economic ​Area.

"I don’t feel that there is bitterness," she said. "I know tempers run high for some people, but I have now spent time with a large group of people from all over the country and people are quite open to different outcomes."

Meanwhile, EU chief Antonio Costa told Frostadottir the bloc "fully respects the democratic choice" of the island's voters not to resume EU membership talks, according to a spokesperson.

"Iceland remains one of the EU's closest and most trusted partners," said the spokesperson for the European Council president.

Iceland opposition: 'This isn't the time'

The count through the night had the island nation on edge as the "Yes" campaign took an early lead, attributable largely to votes in the capital, Reykjavik, before results swung in favor of the opposition.

By dawn, only a few hundred votes separated the two camps before the gap grew as more ballots were tallied in rural areas of the country where opposition was greater.

"This isn't the time to go," one "No" voter, Daniel Bjarkason, told the Associated Press.

"Maybe in 10, 15, 20 years or more, we can take another look. But, for now, we're too divided and that's not a good look. Because it should be 70-30 'Yes' if we're going to [join the EU]."

Neck-and-neck vote after long debate

Iceland has spent the better part of two decades wrestling with the question of becoming a member of the bloc. 

The Nordic country originally applied to join the EU in 2009 following the global financial crisis, which hit the country particularly hard.

Accession talks were suspended in 2013 after a euroskeptic government took office.

Iceland's current left-leaning government, elected in 2024, originally vowed to hold a referendum next year but brought the vote forward because of rising geopolitical tension over Russia's war in Ukraine and Greenland.

Fishing industry pulled weight

The decision puts to bed concerns among many voters that joining the bloc would undermine Iceland's sovereignty, with fishing rights a major concern.

The fisheries sector has been fiercely opposed to joining the bloc, with 90% of industry players against the idea.

The result is a disappointment to Brussels, which had appeared willing to compromise on thorny issues, including fishing and farming, to facilitate Iceland's accession.

entries.title: Greece, Turkey clash over protected Aegean marine areas
entries.summary: Turkey has announced the creation of two protected zones in a disputed area of the Aegean Sea, sparking an angry reaction from Greece. Does this mark a new chapter in a long-running dispute between the two countries?
entries.content:
Greece

Greece, Turkey clash over protected Aegean marine areas

August 30, 2026

Turkey has announced the creation of two protected zones in a disputed area of the Aegean Sea, sparking an angry reaction from Greece. Does this mark a new chapter in a long-running dispute between the two countries?

A stint of unfamiliar calm between Greece and Turkey lasted less than three years.

After a devastating earthquake struck Turkey in February 2023 and Greece provided substantial aid, the two countries came closer together. They then signed the Athens Declaration on Friendly Relations and Good-Neighbourliness in December 2023, a further step to improved relations.

During this unusual time of calm, neither government moved to resolve long-lasting Greek-Turkish disputes, which mostly involve marking maritime boundaries. As a result, even a measure ostensibly aimed at protecting the environment has reignited regional tensions.

The latest dispute was triggered by Turkey's designation of two marine parks in the Aegean Sea and eastern Mediterranean earlier this month. The park in the northeastern Aegean includes a protected area in the waters between the Greek islands of Lemnos and Samothrace. The southern park lies east of Rhodes and surrounds the Greek island of Kastellorizo.

For decades, Greece and Turkey have been at odds over the delineation of their maritime borders in the Aegean and the related economic rights, such as claims to natural resources like oil.

Greece's Foreign Ministry was quick to react to the announcement, calling the establishment of the parks "illegal." In a statement, it said the designation of Turkish marine parks in areas outside Turkey's territorial waters has no legal validity.

Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said at a Cabinet meeting earlier this week that he wanted to maintain good relations with neighboring countries. However, he stressed that "areas under Greek sovereignty are determined by international law" and that Greece is "always ready to defend them."

Competing to protect the Mediterranean?

For its part, Greece also announced two marine parks in 2025 — in the Ionian Islands and the southern Cyclades, both within Greek territorial waters. At the time, Turkey reacted in a clearly worded statement: "Unilateral actions should be avoided in closed or semi-closed seas such as the Aegean and the Mediterranean."

But Turkey has now declared its own marine parks — and without consulting Greece. Environmental protection appears to have been, at most, a secondary concern for the two countries in announcing their respective conservation parks. Instead, the move appears to be a new tactic for asserting dominance in the disputed maritime area — the latest chapter in a decades-long regional spat.

Greece believes Turkey sees the marine parks as a way to challenge the sovereignty of Greek islands. It fears the designation of the two parks is part of Turkey's revisionist "Mavi Vatan" doctrine, Turkish for "Blue Homeland."

Under the doctrine, Turkey lays claim to the exclusive economic zones of Greece and Cyprus — maritime areas in which a coastal state has special rights, including over fishing and the exploitation of natural resources. It also challenges the sovereignty of numerous Greek islands and islets.

Until now, the doctrine has largely remained theoretical and strategic in nature. It is now being advanced through legislative initiatives in Turkey's parliament, and Turkey intends to use the parks to formalize its claims to greater control over parts of the Aegean and eastern Mediterranean.

Greece invests in defense

Greece itself is content with the status quo in the Aegean but feels threatened by Turkey, which is significantly better armed. As a result, Greece has invested heavily in fighter jets, frigates, submarines and air defense systems.

After spending significantly less on arms imports for several years, Greece ranked 19th worldwide among the largest importers of major arms from 2021 to 2025, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.

Even as Athens builds new or closer alliances, Turkey is factored into decisions. In 2021, for example, the Greek government sent Patriot air defense missiles to Saudi Arabia, despite objections from the Greek opposition, to protect Saudi oil refineries from Houthi attacks — at a time when Riyadh and Ankara were at odds politically.

During a state visit with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Prime Minister Mitsotakis explicitly referred to Turkey's "destabilizing and counterproductive" role.

Relations between Ankara and Riyadh have since improved. In early August, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed the Mecca Defense Pact, a major joint defense agreement.

An 'Iron Dome' for Greece

With Turkey in mind, Greece has also pursued strategic cooperation with Israel. Despite heavy criticism in Greece over the dire humanitarian situation in Gaza, Mitsotakis continues to maintain close ties with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The Greek Defense Ministry is planning an air defense shield over the Aegean modeled on Israel's Iron Dome. The project, dubbed the "Achilles Shield," is designed to protect against all conceivable threats — including those from neighboring countries — and is expected to be fully operational by 2029.

For now, Mitsotakis continues to strike a conciliatory tone toward Turkey. But Greece is due to elect a new parliament by spring 2027 at the latest, and Mitsotakis may face growing pressure to take a tougher nationalist stance As the election approaches.

This article was originally written in German.
